name: Speaking and Pronunciation
title: Speaking and Pronunciation
answer: Voice tools can give English learners more speaking practice than a busy classroom allows, and they show real promise for pronunciation when students also get explicit corrective feedback and peer practice. The evidence is strongest for older students, while standard speech recognition remains unreliable for young children because it is trained mostly on adult native speakers. Teachers keep the decisions about topics, level and how the tools are used.

sections.body: Speaking practice is difficult to fit into a crowded classroom, because each student gets only a small amount of time to talk. Voice tools offer a way to increase that practice time. They can also provide feedback on pronunciation, which is otherwise hard for one teacher to give to every student. The idea solves the problem of limited oral practice and limited individual attention. It does not replace the teacher, but it adds repetitions that the school day cannot supply.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, a configured voice tool can be set to use simple language with beginners and more complex language as students advance. The teacher sets clear limits on which topics students may discuss and checks in on how they are using the tool. For older students, the tool can be paired with explicit corrective feedback and peer practice, since that combination produced the gains in the research. For young English learners, teachers should rely on their own ears and use speech tools cautiously, because the technology tends to miss children's errors. The same guardrails described for world language conversation practice apply here.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research support. In a study of 88 ninth graders, students who practiced with a voice assistant that also showed text and graphics improved their speaking more than students who practiced with audio alone or with teachers and peers (Tai, 2022). A meta analysis found a meaningful average effect for pronunciation feedback from speech recognition, but the gains came mostly when students received explicit corrective feedback and practiced with peers (Ngo et al., 2023). Practice with the tool alone, or for a short time, showed little benefit. Detailed feedback on specific sounds worked better than general feedback in a study of 117 high school students (Bashori et al., 2024). Standard speech recognition is trained mostly on adult native speakers and transfers poorly to children learning English, often smoothing over their errors instead of catching them (Michot et al., 2024).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit is that speech recognition is unreliable for young children, so a tool that hears what a child meant rather than what the child said cannot correct pronunciation. Practice with the tool alone, or for only a short time, showed little benefit, so the tool must be combined with explicit corrective feedback and peer practice to matter. The teacher still sets clear limits on topics and checks in on how students are using the tool. The teacher also decides the language level the tool should use and when to rely on their own ears instead. These decisions stay with a person, not the software.
